479	\section{Dotted Method Invocations}
480	\seclabel{dotted-method-calls}
481	
482	\note{Should be a static check that there is an applicable declaration.}
483	
484	\begin{Grammar}
485	\emph{Primary}
486	&::=& \emph{Primary}\EXP{.}\emph{Id}
487	\option{\emph{StaticArgs}} \emph{ParenthesisDelimited}\\
488	
489	\emph{ParenthesisDelimited}
490	&::=& \emph{Parenthesized}\\
491	&$|$& \emph{ArgExpr}\\
492	&$|$& \texttt(\texttt)\\
493	
494	\emph{Parenthesized} &::=& \texttt( \emph{Expr} \texttt)\\
495	
496	\emph{ArgExpr}
497	&::=& \emph{TupleExpr}\\
498	&$|$& \texttt( (\emph{Expr}\EXP{,})$^*$ \emph{Expr}\EXP{...} \texttt)\\
499	
500	\emph{TupleExpr}
501	&::=& \texttt( (\emph{Expr}\EXP{,})$^+$ \emph{Expr} \texttt)\\
502	
503	\end{Grammar}
504	
505	A \emph{dotted method invocation} consists of a subexpression
506	(called the receiver expression), followed by `\txt{.}',
507	followed by an identifier, an optional list of static arguments
508	(described in \chapref{functions})
509	and a subexpression (called the \emph{argument expression}).
510	Unlike in function calls (described in \secref{function-calls}),
511	the argument expression must be parenthesized, even if it is not a tuple.
512	There must be no whitespace on the left-hand side of the `\txt{.}' and
513	the left-hand side of the left parenthesis of the argument expression.
514	The receiver expression evaluates to the receiver of the invocation (bound
515	to the \KWD{self} parameter (discussed in \secref{methods}) of the method).
516	A method invocation may include explicit instantiations of static parameters
517	but most method invocations do not include them; the static arguments
518	are statically inferred from the context of the method invocation (as
519	described in \chapref{type-inference}).
520	
521	The receiver and arguments of a method invocation are each evaluated
522	in parallel in a separate implicit thread (see
523	\secref{threads-parallelism}).  After this thread group completes
524	normally, the body of the method is evaluated with the parameter of
525	the method bound to the value of the argument expression (thus
526	evaluation of the body occurs after evaluation of the receiver and
527	arguments in dynamic program order).  The value and the type of a
528	dotted method invocation are the value and the type of the method
529	body.
530	
531	We say that methods or functions (collectively called as
532	\emph{functionals}) may be \emph{applied to}
533	(also ``\emph{invoked on}'' or ``\emph{called with}'') an argument.
534	We use ``call'', ``invocation'', and ``application'' interchangeably.
535

/**
 * A convenient type for an actual type checker instance for use in Java
 * code. This class mixes all the implementation into the abstract base class.
 */
class STypeCheckerImpl(current: CompilationUnitIndex,
                       traits: TraitTable,
                       env: STypeEnv,
                       labelExitTypes: JavaMap[Id, Option[JavaSet[Type]]],
                       errors: ErrorLog)
                      (implicit analyzer: TypeAnalyzer,
                                envCache: MMap[APIName, STypeEnv],
                                cycleChecker: CyclicReferenceChecker)
    extends STypeChecker(current, traits, env, labelExitTypes, errors)
    with Dispatch with Common
    with Decls with Functionals with Operators
    with Misc {

  override def constructor(current: CompilationUnitIndex,
                           traits: TraitTable,
                           env: STypeEnv,
                           labelExitTypes: JavaMap[Id, Option[JavaSet[Type]]],
                           errors: ErrorLog)
                          (implicit analyzer: TypeAnalyzer,
                                    envCache: MMap[APIName, STypeEnv],
                                    cycleChecker: CyclicReferenceChecker) =
  new STypeCheckerImpl(current, traits, env, labelExitTypes, errors)

}

/**
 * The abstract base class for a type checker. This class contains all the
 * basic functionality for use in type checking, including helper methods that
 * are widely used for many different cases. Use the `STypeCheckerImpl` class
 * instead for a fully implemented type checker.
 *
 * The actual type checking is defined abstractly; concrete subclasses or mixed-
 * in traits should provide the actual implementation of type checking each
 * case.
 *
 * Constructor parameters are marked `protected val` so that the implementing,
 * mixed-in traits can access the fields.
 */
abstract class STypeChecker(val current: CompilationUnitIndex,
                            val traits: TraitTable,
                            val env: STypeEnv,
                            val labelExitTypes: JavaMap[Id, Option[JavaSet[Type]]],
                            val errors: ErrorLog)
                           (implicit val analyzer: TypeAnalyzer,
                                     val envCache: MMap[APIName, STypeEnv],
                                     val cycleChecker: CyclicReferenceChecker) {

  /** Oracle for determining coercions between types. */
  protected implicit val coercions = new CoercionOracle(traits, current)

  /**
   * This method simply creates a new instance of the class in which it is defined. We need this
   * so that subclasses will extend themselves properly. This MUST be overriden in every subclass of
   * STypeChecker.
   */
  def constructor(current: CompilationUnitIndex,
                  traits: TraitTable,
                  env: STypeEnv,
                  labelExitTypes: JavaMap[Id, Option[JavaSet[Type]]],                  errors: ErrorLog)
                 (implicit analyzer: TypeAnalyzer,
                           envCache: MMap[APIName, STypeEnv],
                           cycleChecker: CyclicReferenceChecker): STypeCheckerImpl

  def extend(newEnv: STypeEnv, newAnalyzer: TypeAnalyzer) =
    constructor(current, traits, newEnv, labelExitTypes, errors)(newAnalyzer, envCache, cycleChecker)

  def extend(bindings: List[Binding]) =
    constructor(current,
                traits,
                env.extend(bindings),
                labelExitTypes,
                errors)

  def extend(sparams: List[StaticParam], where: Option[WhereClause]) =
    constructor(current,
                traits,
                env,
                labelExitTypes,
                errors)(analyzer.extend(sparams, where), envCache, cycleChecker)

  def extend(sparams: List[StaticParam],
             params: Option[List[Param]],
             where: Option[WhereClause]) = {
    val newEnv = params match {
      case Some(ps) => env.extend(ps)
      case None => env
    }
    constructor(current,
                traits,
                newEnv,
                labelExitTypes,
                errors)(analyzer.extend(sparams, where), envCache, cycleChecker)
  }

  def extend(id: Id, typ: Type): STypeChecker =
    extend(List[LValue](NodeFactory.makeLValue(id, typ)))

  def extend(ids: List[Id], types: List[Type]): STypeChecker =
    extend(ids.zip(types).map((p:(Id, Type)) =>
        NodeFactory.makeLValue(p._1,p._2)))

  def extend(id_types: List[(Id, Type)]): STypeChecker =
    extend(id_types.map((p:(Id, Type)) =>
        NodeFactory.makeLValue(p._1,p._2)))

  def extend(decl: LocalVarDecl): STypeChecker =
    constructor(current,
                traits,
                env.extend(decl),
                labelExitTypes,
                errors)

  def extendWithFunctions[T <: Functional](methods: Relation[IdOrOpOrAnonymousName, T]) =
    constructor(current,
                traits,
                env.extendWithFunctions(methods),
                labelExitTypes,
                errors)

  def extendWithListOfFunctions[T <: Functional](fns:List[T]) =
    constructor(current,
                traits,
                env.extendWithListOfFunctions(fns),
                labelExitTypes,
                errors)

  def extendWithout(declSite: Node, names: Set[Id]) =
    constructor(current,
                traits,
                env.extendWithout(names),
                labelExitTypes,
                errors)

  def addSelf(self_type: Type) =
    extend(List[LValue](NodeFactory.makeLValue("self", self_type)))

  protected def signal(msg:String, hasAt:HasAt) =
    errors.signal(msg, hasAt)

  protected def signal(hasAt:HasAt, msg:String) =
    errors.signal(msg, hasAt)

  protected def signal(error: StaticError) =
    errors.signal(error)

  protected def syntaxError(hasAt:HasAt, msg:String) =
    error(hasAt, msg)

  protected def isValidErrorMessage(msg: String) = !msg.containsSlice("%s")

entries.name: TaskCreate
entries.description:
Use this tool to create a structured task list for your current coding session. This helps you track progress, organize complex tasks, and demonstrate thoroughness to the user.
It also helps the user understand the progress of the task and overall progress of their requests.

## When to Use This Tool

Use this tool proactively in these scenarios:

- Complex multi-step tasks - When a task requires 3 or more distinct steps or actions
- Non-trivial and complex tasks - Tasks that require careful planning or multiple operations
- Plan mode - When using plan mode, create a task list to track the work
- User explicitly requests todo list - When the user directly asks you to use the todo list
- User provides multiple tasks - When users provide a list of things to be done (numbered or comma-separated)
- After receiving new instructions - Immediately capture user requirements as tasks
- When you start working on a task - Mark it as in_progress BEFORE beginning work
- After completing a task - Mark it as completed and add any new follow-up tasks discovered during implementation

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Skip using this tool when:
- There is only a single, straightforward task
- The task is trivial and tracking it provides no organizational benefit
- The task can be completed in less than 3 trivial steps
- The task is purely conversational or informational

NOTE that you should not use this tool if there is only one trivial task to do. In this case you are better off just doing the task directly.

## Task Fields

- **subject**: A brief, actionable title in imperative form (e.g., "Fix authentication bug in login flow")
- **description**: What needs to be done
- **activeForm** (optional): Present continuous form shown in the spinner when the task is in_progress (e.g., "Fixing authentication bug"). If omitted, the spinner shows the subject instead.

All tasks are created with status `pending`.

## Tips

- Create tasks with clear, specific subjects that describe the outcome
- After creating tasks, use TaskUpdate to set up dependencies (blocks/blockedBy) if needed
- Check TaskList first to avoid creating duplicate tasks

entries.name: TaskUpdate
entries.description:
Use this tool to update a task in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

**Mark tasks as resolved:**
- When you have completed the work described in a task
- When a task is no longer needed or has been superseded
- IMPORTANT: Always mark your assigned tasks as resolved when you finish them
- After resolving, call TaskList to find your next task

- ONLY mark a task as completed when you have FULLY accomplished it
- If you encounter errors, blockers, or cannot finish, keep the task as in_progress
- When blocked, create a new task describing what needs to be resolved
- Never mark a task as completed if:
  - Tests are failing
  - Implementation is partial
  - You encountered unresolved errors
  - You couldn't find necessary files or dependencies

**Delete tasks:**
- When a task is no longer relevant or was created in error
- Setting status to `deleted` permanently removes the task

**Update task details:**
- When requirements change or become clearer
- When establishing dependencies between tasks

## Fields You Can Update

- **status**: The task status (see Status Workflow below)
- **subject**: Change the task title (imperative form, e.g., "Run tests")
- **description**: Change the task description
- **activeForm**: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")
- **owner**: Change the task owner (agent name)
- **metadata**: Merge metadata keys into the task (set a key to null to delete it)
- **addBlocks**: Mark tasks that cannot start until this one completes
- **addBlockedBy**: Mark tasks that must complete before this one can start

## Status Workflow

Status progresses: `pending` → `in_progress` → `completed`

Use `deleted` to permanently remove a task.

## Staleness

Make sure to read a task's latest state using `TaskGet` before updating it.

## Examples

Mark task as in progress when starting work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "in_progress"}
```

Mark task as completed after finishing work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "completed"}
```

Delete a task:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "deleted"}
```

Claim a task by setting owner:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "owner": "my-name"}
```

Set up task dependencies:
```json
{"taskId": "2", "addBlockedBy": ["1"]}
```

addBlocks.description: Task IDs that this task blocks

addBlockedBy.description: Task IDs that block this task

(* An operator repeated between three operands has the expected type of its value, whether a multifix declaration accepts it or it is left-associated, so that type fixes a static argument that only the result mentions. *)
component InferRepeatedOperatorContext
export Executable

object BoxV[\T\](v: T) end
opr OPLUS[\T\](a: Any, b: ZZ32): BoxV[\T\] = throw InvalidRange
opr OTIMES[\T\](a: ZZ32, b: ZZ32, c: ZZ32): BoxV[\T\] = throw IntegerDomainError
binary(): String = try
    y: BoxV[\ZZ64\] = 1 OPLUS 2 OPLUS 3
    "value"

    "value"

  end

## B.6 Type checking

`TypeCheckPhase` builds indexes for the apis and components, checks the apis, then the components (`phases/TypeCheckPhase.java:32-58`); the work is in `StaticChecker.checkCompilationUnit` (`compiler/StaticChecker.java:163`).

For an api: compound-api check, api linking, type-hierarchy acyclicity, well-formedness (`:174-220`).

For a component: `ApiTypeExtractor`, `TypeNormalizer`, a `TraitTable` and a `TypeAnalyzer`, then `Thunker` to give elided return types thunks, then `STypeChecker.typeCheck` (`:196-247`), then well-formedness again, overloading rules, export checking and the variance checker (`:268-290`).

The checker writes a type onto each expression node and produces no new representation, which is why the same `nodes/` tree continues into DESUGAR.

The variance checker is skipped when `compiled_expr_desugaring` is off, with the comment "Hack: don't run the variance checker if running the interpreter" (`StaticChecker.java:289-290`) — one of the few places in the checker that names the interpreter at all.

`Shell.getScala()` selects between the Scala checker and a Java one that no longer exists (`StaticChecker.java:228-230`); `setScala(false)` is set by `walk` (`Shell.java:422`), `typecheck-old` (`:467`), `test` (`:475`), the bare-filename arm (`:481`) and the `-typecheck-java` flag (`:865`).

1984	\subsection{The contexts that give a call an expected type}
1985	\seclabel{revival-expected-contexts}
1986	
1987	\begin{description}
1988	\item[Affected sections] \secref{static-arg-inference}; \secref{numeral-default}.
1989	\item[Change] The list of the contexts in which a call has an expected type,
1990	in \secref{static-arg-inference}, gives the last expression of a block the
1991	block's expected type whether or not local declarations precede it, and gains
1992	two contexts: a clause of an \KWD{if} expression without an \KWD{else} clause,
1993	whose expected type is \TYP{()}, and a clause of a \KWD{typecase} expression
1994	that has an expected type, its \KWD{else} clause among them, whose expected
1995	type is that of the \KWD{typecase} expression.
1996	The sentence after the list says that the expected type is used also for a call
1997	written by loose juxtaposition, as \EXP{f\;x}.
1998	The item of the list of what the chapter does not yet describe, in
1999	\secref{numeral-default}, names an argument of another call, the body of a
2000	\KWD{for} loop and the body of a \KWD{label} expression, and no longer names
2001	the contexts that the list of contexts now gives.
2002	Each changed passage has a box.
2003	How a call is instantiated under its expected type is unchanged.
2004	\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; it follows the
2005	revival's decision of 8~October 2026 that these four contexts give a call the
2006	type that the text already requires of them, a clause of a \KWD{typecase}
2007	expression by the rule for the type of the \KWD{typecase} expression.
2008	The text gives each context its type.
2009	``If there is no \KWD{else} clause in an \KWD{if} expression, then every clause
2010	must have type \EXP{()}'' (\secref{if-expr}).
2011	``If the last element of the expression block is an expression, the value and
2012	type of this expression are the value and type of the expression block as a
2013	whole'' (\secref{block-expr}), whatever local declarations precede it.
2014	The static arguments of an identifier reference ``are statically inferred from
2015	the context of the function call'' (\secref{idn-ref}), however the call is
2016	written.
2017	``The type of a \KWD{typecase} expression is the union of types of all
2018	right-hand sides of the typecase clauses'' (\secref{typecase}), which is a
2019	subtype of the expected type when the type of each clause is.
2020	Since the revival's decision of 29~September 2026 a type parameter that nothing
2021	at a call fixes takes the intersection of its upper bounds, never
2022	\TYP{BottomType} (\secref{revival-inference}), so a call of \VAR{fail} or
2023	\VAR{builtinPrimitive} of \library, whose type parameter only the result
2024	mentions, took the bound \TYP{Any} in these contexts, and the compiled type
2025	checker refused thirteen such calls of \library\ that the interpreter runs
2026	(row~560 of the revival's gap ledger).
2027	The alternative not taken was that the library write the static argument at
2028	each such call, as \EXP{\VAR{fail}\llbracket()\rrbracket(s)}: the revival
2029	decided that the library's own practice is the standard, and the library does
2030	not route round a gap of the type checker.
2031	A reversal would take the four contexts out of the list of contexts and back
2032	into the item, and the compiled type checker would refuse those calls again.
2033	The full reasoning is in
2034	\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-checker-expected-type/REPORT.md}
2035	in the revival's repository.
2036	\item[Effect] The compiled type checker gives these contexts their expected
2037	types: it checks a clause of an \KWD{if} expression without an \KWD{else}
2038	clause against \TYP{()}, and it gives the expected type of the enclosing
2039	expression to the last expression of a block after local declarations, to a
2040	clause of a \KWD{typecase} expression and to the application that a loose
2041	juxtaposition makes.
2042	Twelve of the thirteen calls of \library\ that it refused now check.
2043	It still gives no expected type to an argument of another call (row~455 of the
2044	revival's gap ledger) or to the body of a \KWD{label} expression (row~642),
2045	as the item of the list says; the thirteenth call ends a clause of a
2046	\KWD{typecase} expression that ends the body of a \KWD{label} expression.
2047	Nor does it give one to an operator repeated between three or more operands
2048	that no multifix declaration accepts, as \EXP{p \oplus q \oplus r}, though the
2049	outer of the binary applications \EXP{(p \oplus q) \oplus r} that it stands for
2050	is an operator application, which the sentence after the list gives the
2051	expected type (row~644).
2052	The interpreter has no static types and is unchanged.
2053	\item[Original text] The two passages are the revival's own text of
2054	29~September 2026, not the Working Draft's, whose chapter held a heading and two
2055	draft notes (\secref{revival-inference}).
2056	The list of contexts said, in \nolinkurl{Specification/basic/inference.tex},
2057	lines 129--139, before this revision:
2058	\begin{quote}
2059	A call has an expected type in these contexts: as the right-hand side of a
2060	variable or field declaration that declares its type, that type; as the
2061	right-hand side of an assignment to a variable whose type is declared, that
2062	type; as the body of a functional that declares its return type, that type;
2063	as the last expression of a block that has an expected type, where no local
2064	declaration precedes it in the block, the block's expected type; and as a
2065	branch of an \KWD{if} expression with an \KWD{else} clause that has an
2066	expected type, the expected type of the \KWD{if} expression.
2067	The expected type is used whether the call is written by tight juxtaposition,
2068	as \EXP{f(x)} (\secref{juxtameaning}), or as a method invocation or an operator
2069	application.
2070	\end{quote}
2071	The item of the list of what the chapter does not yet describe said, in lines
2072	254--258:
2073	\begin{quote}
2074	an expected type in any context other than those listed above, such as
2075	an argument of another call, an expression that a local declaration precedes in
2076	a block, an \KWD{if} expression without an \KWD{else} clause, a \KWD{typecase}
2077	expression, the body of a \KWD{for} loop, or a call written by loose
